rule: Design websites with low visual complexity and high prototypicality to maximize perceived aesthetic appeal.
quote: websites with low VC and high PT were perceived as highly appealing
finding: Low visual complexity and high prototypicality rated highest for aesthetics across 50ms to 1000ms exposure times

rule: Group related UI elements together to reduce navigation time for screen reader users.
quote: grouped relevant UI elements together to save navigation time for screen reader users

rule: Scope all code generation interactions explicitly to guarantee what portions of the UI will and will not be mutated.
quote: All interactions are explicitly scoped, with guarantees on what portions of the UI will and will not be mutated
finding: Developers rated perceived control as high and usability as positive when using explicitly scoped affordances

rule: Customize interface content and features based on user expertise level and context to improve comprehension.
quote: explaining the microbiome to a 5 year old requires different content and a different set of features than explaining it to an adult

rule: Use dark gray or navy backgrounds instead of pure black to reduce eye strain while maintaining contrast.
quote: consider using a very dark gray or navy blue background, which provides enough contrast but is easier on the eyes

rule: Ensure high contrast between UI elements and backgrounds, especially in dark mode where the color palette is limited.
quote: UI elements, such as buttons or text, need to have high-contrast colors that are easily distinguishable from each other. This is especially important in dark mode

rule: Test your interface designs thoroughly in both light and dark modes before release.
quote: Test your design thoroughly to ensure it works well in both light and dark modes

rule: Provide users with a toggle option to switch between light and dark modes rather than forcing one mode.
quote: make sure to provide an option to switch between light and dark modes. You can achieve this through a simple toggle switch or syncing with the device's system settings

rule: Reduce color saturation in dark mode to prevent colors from appearing too bright or overpowering.
quote: Colors with high saturation can appear too bright or overpowering in dark mode. To avoid this issue, consider using less saturated colors

rule: Ensure images and icons remain visible against dark backgrounds by using sufficient contrast.
quote: ensure they remain visible and don't blend into the background by using colors that provide enough contrast

rule: Offer dark mode when users spend extended time in your product or use it in varying lighting environments.
quote: Offer a dark mode option when your users spend a lot of time in your product or use it in different lighting environments

rule: Place error messages next to or below the field causing the error, not in separate summaries.
quote: Keeping error messages next to the fields in error minimizes working-memory load: users can see the error message while fixing the error instead of having to remember it.

rule: Use color plus iconography to mark errors, not color alone, to support colorblind users.
quote: Add a semitransparent background of the same color to the error field to make it stand out on a long page with many form fields.

rule: Show success indicators for complex fields like passwords to guide users without repeated guessing.
quote: For complex inputs such as new passwords, instant inline validation (which appears as the field value is being typed) will prevent users from guessing or checking multiple times if what they've entered meets the system's guidelines.

rule: Organize layouts with simplicity, organization, and coherence to avoid cognitive overload.
quote: Users prefer clean, simple layouts that are easy to understand at a glance. Overly complicated designs can lead to cognitive overload, making it difficult for users to navigate or find important information.

rule: Use skeleton screens for content loading to improve perceived performance over blank screens.
quote: Unlike preloader animations and progress bars, skeleton loading screens improve perceived performance well since users can feel how data segments will appear on the screen even though they are not yet loaded.

rule: Use animated skeleton loaders for content loading over one second to maintain user engagement.
quote: Most designers choose animated skeleton loaders since they indicate the loading state effectively and keep the user engaged even if the loading time expands over about one second.

rule: Use skeleton screens when fetching content and layout context matters, like feeds or dashboards.
quote: Go for a skeleton screen when content is being fetched, and layout context matters, such as feeds, dashboards, search results, or product listings.

rule: Use spinners for short, blocking actions like form submission or authentication, not content loading.
quote: Use a spinner for short or blocking actions such as submitting a form, authentication, saving, processing, or payments.

rule: Show visible loading feedback within 50 milliseconds to prevent users interpreting the interface as broken.
quote: Research indicates that nearly 90% of users anticipate some form of interactive feedback — whether a hover response, visual state change, or loading indicator — within about 50 milliseconds of an action.
finding: 90% of users expect feedback within 50 milliseconds

rule: Display skeleton screens that mimic the final layout to help users recognize content structure immediately.
quote: Because the placeholders match the final structure, users can scan the page instantly. They recognize a feed, a product listing, or a dashboard before the content arrives.

rule: Provide flexible user control so users can pause, review, and interact via keyboard, voice, or assistive tech.
quote: Support device-independent interaction. Let users pause, review, and control the experience using their preferred input—keyboard, voice, or others.

rule: Write error messages in plain language that tells users exactly what is wrong and how to fix it.
quote: Provide clear, descriptive error messages in plain language. Make sure feedback is timely, visible, and helps users recover smoothly.

rule: Add text labels or alternatives for icon-only buttons so all users understand their function.
quote: An icon-only button may confuse some users. Adding a text label like "Save" or "Download report" helps clarify the function, even without visuals.

rule: Organize form fields in a logical order that reflects natural task flow, not arbitrary groupings.
quote: A logical flow—email → shipping → payment—keeps the process clear.

rule: Build accessibility into reusable components with keyboard support and clear roles from the start.
quote: Create reusable UI components with accessibility built in—keyboard support, clear roles, alternative equivalents—and use them consistently.

rule: Design websites with low visual complexity and high prototypicality to maximize initial beauty perception.
quote: users strongly prefer website designs that look both simple (low complexity) and familiar (high prototypicality)
finding: Users form aesthetic judgments in 17–50 milliseconds; negative first impressions reduce satisfaction

rule: Avoid designs contradicting user expectations, as they damage first impressions and product satisfaction.
quote: Designs that contradict what users typically expect of a website may hurt users' first impression and damage their expectations

rule: Use microinteractions to provide immediate feedback confirming user actions and reducing cognitive load.
quote: Microinteractions improve usability by giving users immediate feedback on their actions, making the interface feel responsive and alive

rule: Provide non-visual alternatives like sound, vibration, or text for color-only microinteraction feedback.
quote: Adding alternative cues like sound, vibration, or text descriptions ensures that everyone receives the necessary feedback

rule: Make focus states clear and easily identifiable for keyboard and assistive-device users.
quote: Clear, easily identifiable focus indicators help these users track their progress through a webpage

rule: Keep microinteractions simple, quick, and purpose-driven to avoid overwhelming or distracting users.
quote: Microinteractions should be quick, subtle, and purpose-driven, not over-the-top or distracting

rule: Use spatial motion to orient users about location, direction, and how to navigate back.
quote: Spacial motion design applies our basic understanding of physical space and translates it into a digital system to help the user remember where they are, how they move forward, and how to get back

rule: Ensure screen readers detect animated events, state changes, and overlays to prevent missing critical information.
quote: Screen readers can miss events like partial page loads, temporary animated overlays (like toasts or banners), and animated state changes

rule: Keep motion design moderate to prevent dizziness and disorientation in users with vestibular disorders.
quote: People with vestibular disorders may experience motion design in an interface to be very unpleasant, nauseating, and/or disorienting to various degrees

rule: Avoid drastic or fast motion that increases cognitive load by confusing object associations.
quote: Motion design that is either too drastic, fast, or both can cause confusion and add to a user's cognitive load

rule: Position animated notifications on-screen for low-vision users with screen magnification.
quote: If animated events like a notification or toast come in and appear off screen, the user may not see it

rule: Increase line spacing as a percentage when using smaller font sizes.
quote: Line spacing as a % should actually increase with smaller font sizes. This is because smaller fonts are already more difficult to read

rule: Re-check line spacing when changing font or font size to maintain readability.
quote: Different fonts have different maximum heights (x-heights) even when they're the same size in points. So you need to be sure that when you change font, you check to see how your line spacing feels

rule: Start with 17px mobile body font size and adjust based on content density and readability.
quote: the best rule of thumb: start with size 17, and adjust from there

rule: Make secondary text 2px smaller than default paragraph text.
quote: For secondary text – like lesser labels, captions, etc. – use a size a couple notches smaller – such as 13px or 14px

rule: View font-size designs on actual mobile devices to validate readability.
quote: The gold standard of choosing mobile font sizes is to view your designs on an actual device

rule: Remove unnecessary form fields to increase completion rates and submission accuracy.
quote: Every time you cut a field or question from a form, you increase its conversion rate
finding: Forms following usability guidelines: 78% one-try submissions; violating: 42%

rule: Place labels immediately above or adjacent to their fields with minimal ambiguous spacing.
quote: Labels should be close to the fields they describe (immediately above the field for mobile and shorter desktop forms, or next to the field for extremely long desktop forms). Avoid ambiguous spacing

rule: List most-frequently-used values first in option lists.
quote: for field values, also consider usage frequency, and list the most common values first when possible

rule: Never use Reset or Clear buttons; they increase accidental data loss.
quote: to avoid Reset buttons on web forms

rule: Avoid placeholder text as labels; use explicit labels instead.
quote: Avoid placeholder text

rule: Don't put vital task information in tooltips; use persistent labels for field requirements.
quote: Users shouldn't need to find a tooltip in order to complete their task. Tooltips are best when they provide additional explanation for a form field unfamiliar to some users

rule: Write brief, helpful tooltip text that adds value; omit tooltips with obvious or redundant content.
quote: Tooltips with obvious or redundant text are not beneficial to users. If you can't think of particularly helpful content, don't offer a tooltip.

rule: Support tooltip activation via keyboard focus as well as mouse hover.
quote: Tooltips that appear only on mouse hover are inaccessible for users that rely on keyboards to navigate. Be inclusive in your design and ensure that your tooltips are accessible via keyboards.

rule: Use arrows to clarify tooltip associations when multiple interactive elements are nearby.
quote: Arrows are beneficial to clearly identify to which element the tooltip is associated. When there are several nearby elements, these arrows help avoid confusion.

rule: Define animation purpose before adding it: clarify whether it attracts attention, shows state transitions, or indicates relationships.
quote: Before adding animations to a web page or application, ensure that their goal and purpose are well defined.

rule: Use slow fades for less disruptive animations; sliding motion attracts attention faster and should be reserved for critical alerts.
quote: Elements that slide in or otherwise display a shift in position at any degree of speed will attract attention faster than elements that slowly fade into place.

rule: Provide automated UI detection with 71.3% mean average precision to assist screen reader users accessing poorly labeled apps.
quote: our UI detection model achieved 71.3% mean AP
finding: 71.3% mean average precision on 5,002 test screenshots across 13 UI element types

rule: Recognize UI selection states visually using tint color and detection type to communicate toggles and checkboxes to assistive devices.
quote: We leveraged their visual information to determine the selection states (tint color, UI detection type, and so on)
finding: 90.5% recall for tab button selection state, 73.6% for segmented controls

rule: Generate UI interfaces that adapt complexity, content, and feature set to user expertise level and context for improved comprehension.
quote: It customizes the experience with an understanding that explaining the microbiome to a 5 year old requires different content and a different set of features than explaining it to an adult

rule: Configure consistent visual styling across all generated UI results to establish recognizable product identity and user expectations.
quote: For some products, it might be preferable to consistently see results in specific styles. Our implementation could be configured for these products so that all results, including generated assets, are created in a consistent style for all users.

rule: Prioritize generation quality over speed; human-expert designs are preferred, but fast generative UI is acceptable when speed is critical.
quote: This evaluation did not take into account generation speed. We also show that the performance of generative UI strongly depends on the performance of the underlying model
finding: generative UI strongly preferred after expert sites; performance depends on model quality

rule: Pair all color-based feedback with non-visual cues like text, icons, or borders to ensure users with color blindness perceive microinteraction state changes.
quote: combine color changes with other visual cues like text, icons, or borders to make actions clear

rule: Ensure touch targets meet a minimum size of 44×44 pixels to accommodate users with limited dexterity across mobile and touchscreen devices.
quote: typically aiming for a minimum size of 44px by 44px
finding: 44 pixels by 44 pixels minimum touch target size

rule: Provide haptic and auditory feedback on mobile devices alongside visual feedback to serve users with visual impairments or limited sight.
quote: haptic feedback (vibration) and auditory cues are essential for accessibility, especially for users with visual impairments or limited mobility

rule: Respect prefers-reduced-motion system settings and ensure microinteraction functionality is preserved when motion is disabled.
quote: Ensure that microinteractions are still functional and provide feedback when motion is reduced or disabled

rule: Limit microinteraction complexity and frequency to avoid overwhelming users with cognitive disabilities or sensory sensitivities.
quote: By designing clear and familiar interactions (e.g., progress indicators for loading times or error messages), users with cognitive challenges can more easily understand what's happening

rule: Let users trigger motion through actions rather than auto-playing animations.
quote: Motion design is best when it is subtle and happens after a user has taken an action. Motion design that auto-plays or is unexpected can be unpleasant for many people.

rule: Keep animation at the point of focus to direct attention without distracting users.
quote: Animation should be used to direct a user's attention to the most important thing on the screen that they may need to interact with.

rule: Forms with usability guidelines achieve 78% one-try error-free submissions versus 42% for non-compliant forms.
quote: 78% one-try submissions in forms compliant with usability guidelines versus only 42% one-try submissions in forms violating them

rule: Present form fields in a single column to maintain vertical momentum; avoid multi-column layouts that disrupt user flow.
quote: Multiple columns interrupt the vertical momentum of moving down the form. Rather than requiring users to visually reorient themselves, keep them in the flow by sticking to a single column

rule: Size text input fields to match expected input length, empirically: 19 characters fits 99.9% of city names.
quote: 99.9% of city names were 19 characters or shorter, making 19 characters a reasonable width for a city field
finding: 19-character field width accommodates 99.9% of city names

rule: Signal errors with multiple non-color cues: outline the field AND use red text AND use heavier font weight.
quote: Errors should be signaled through a variety of cues, not solely through color: outline the field AND use red text AND use a heavier font

rule: Avoid showing validation errors before the user finishes typing; wait until they move to the next field.
quote: In most cases, avoid showing an error until the user has finished with the field and moved to the next field. It's frustrating to see an error message before being given the opportunity to finish typing

rule: When users encounter the same error 3+ times, address the root cause: unclear messages, design mismatch, or overly complex requirements.
quote: When users encounter the same error repeatedly (3 or more times in a single form-filling attempt), it indicates a deeper issue in the user interface

rule: Use consistent visual styling for buttons and links with the same function to signal they behave identically.
quote: Style all buttons or links that perform similar functions the same way (e.g., same color, size, and shape)

rule: Balance contrast carefully: too much overwhelms users, too little makes designs feel monotonous and hard to navigate.
quote: Too much contrast can overwhelm users, while too little can make the design feel monotonous or difficult to navigate. Striking the perfect balance here is the secret sauce to maintaining simplicity in UI UX

rule: Begin animations within 0.1 seconds of user action to maintain direct manipulation feeling.
quote: the effect must begin within 0.1 seconds of the initial user action. This 0.1-second response time maintains the feeling of direct manipulation

rule: Avoid repeating animations on frequently accessed UI elements; users find them annoying after first encounter.
quote: this [animation] was nice the first time, but now it's getting annoying

rule: Match skeleton layout exactly to the final loaded screen so users immediately recognize content structure and section positions.
quote: A skeleton screen should be consistent in layout and structure with the final loaded screen. This gives users an idea of what the final screen will look like, as well as where to potentially find the type of content they are looking for.

rule: Exclude smaller UI elements like buttons, form fields, and labels from skeleton screens; use placeholders only for primary structural components.
quote: Skeleton screens are more focused on structure and layout while excluding the smaller details, like icons or status indicators.

rule: Use skeleton screens for container-based components like cards, tiles, grids, and data tables; avoid them for smaller components.
quote: Skeleton screens primarily work best when loading container-based components, such as tiles, structured lists, grids, data tables, and card components.

rule: Use distinguishable colors and clear but undistracted animations in skeleton screens to support accessibility and visibility.
quote: Choosing distinguishable colors for skeleton screens' placeholders and implementing clear but undistracted animations is the best way to clearly indicate the loading state by prioritizing accessibility.

rule: Use skeleton screens for content-heavy interfaces where layout context and content anticipation matter, such as feeds, dashboards, and product listings.
quote: You can use a spinner for short or blocking actions such as submitting a form, authentication, saving, processing, or payments. But go for a skeleton screen when content is being fetched, and layout context matters, such as feeds, dashboards, search results, or product listings.

rule: Implement progressive loading in skeleton screens so placeholders transform into real content, making users perceive the interface as faster.
quote: A skeleton screen makes progress visible. As placeholders transform into real content, users experience continuous advancement. Even if both interfaces take the same number of seconds to load, the one with the skeleton screen is usually perceived as faster because users see incremental change rather than a single reveal.

rule: Organize form fields in a logical order that reflects natural task flow, such as email, shipping address, then payment information.
quote: A checkout form that asks for payment info before contact details can confuse users. A logical flow—email → shipping → payment—keeps the process clear.

rule: Avoid pure black backgrounds; use dark gray or navy instead to reduce eye strain.
quote: Avoid pure black backgrounds: While pure black backgrounds may seem like a good fit for dark mode, they can be too harsh on the eyes. Instead, consider using a very dark gray or navy blue background

rule: Dark mode has no measured performance benefit in daytime or well-lit conditions; its value is aesthetic and contextual.
quote: The results revealed no significant differences between dark and light modes in terms of productivity or error rates. The significance of this study lies in its challenge to common assumptions about dark mode's functional benefits, emphasizing that its popularity may be driven more by aesthetics and personal preference
finding: No significant differences in productivity or error rates between dark and light modes in well-lit daytime conditions

rule: Reduce labeler decision space by showing only the most probable label recommendations; this improves speed and accuracy.
quote: providing assistance via a label recommendation reduced the labeler's decision space by focusing their attention on only the most probable labels. This technique improved labelers' speed and accuracy, especially when the labeler found the correct label in the reduced label space.
finding: Label recommendation interface improved labelers' speed and accuracy by reducing decision space

rule: Use confidence highlighting and alternate options to help users detect and correct errors in AI-generated code.
quote: UI features such as confidence highlighting and alternate translations can help software engineers work productively with generative NMT models.

rule: Deploy tooltips consistently for all similar elements, not just some, or users will not discover them and expectations will break.
quote: If tooltips are erratically displayed throughout your site, people may never discover them. It's important to be consistent and provide tooltips for all the elements in your design rather than just for some.
